newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian metal demand sluggish, offtake low.
newsitem.headline: Indian metal demand sluggish, offtake low.

text.p: Demand for Indian domestic non-ferrous metals was sluggish during the week due to lower offtake and increased import arrivals, dealers said on Wednesday.
"The market is a little slack, there is no offtake," said Ashok Basna, director of the Bombay Metals Exchange.

Dealers said offtake was low because the domestic automobile and engineering industries were not making expected purchases. They said imports of finished goods were preferred because of the duty parity between raw material and finished products.
"Copper, Zinc and aluminium prices are steady but they have been sold below cost price for the last six months," said Surendra Parikh, a leading metals trader.
Traders said demand for metals was expected to pick up with the passage of the 1997/98 (April/March) budget. Government agencies normally place orders soon after the budget, they said.

The Indian parliament on Wednesday approved Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's path-breaking budget that slashed taxes and tariffs. The budget proposed to double import duty on aluminium ingots to 20 percent to protect the domestic industry. But it left other metals duties largely untouched.

In the parliamentary debate on Wednesday, Chidambaram said he proposed to cut import duty on ferro-nickel to 10 percent from 20 percent. Chidambaram said the measure was being taken to provide relief to the steel industry.
Parikh said with the increase in aluminium duties domestic prices of the metal were cheaper and imports had dwindled.
"Every month 5,000 tonnes of aluminium were arriving. Now there is no scope, nobody is importing," Parikh said.
Parikh said LME prices were steady and there was not much fluctuation.
India meets most of its non-ferrous metals requirements through imports, and LME prices have a direct bearing on the local market.
